question: A basic inverting integrator using OP-AMP is unstable at low frequencies. What modification is commonly made to stabilise it?

options.text: Add a resistor in series with the capacitor in the feedback path
Add a resistor in parallel with the capacitor in the feedback path

solution:
__**Op-Amp Integrator:**__

 
• It is on operational Amplifier circuit that performs mathematical operation of Integration with respect to time.
 
• Its output voltage is proportional to the input voltage integrated over time

{V₀} propto mathop smallint limits₀^t {V_i}dt

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/de43c936f4ffaa53eb7f391cf975df7bbdff3cc1df254b57f22ea32cf0ddbfe2.png] 

 
• When step input (Vᵢ) is given to the circuit –
 
• It performs integration and output is a triangular wave with dc bias.
 
• When a step voltage Vᵢ is applied to the input of an integrating amplifier, the uncharged capacitor ‘C’ (has very little resistance) acts as a short circuit allowing maximum current to flow.
 
• As the impedance of the capacitor is very small then the gain ratio is also very small (XC/R₁) and the overall voltage gain is less than 1.
 
• (i.e. voltage follower circuit)
 
• Feedback capacitor C begins to charge up due to Vᵢ and impedance XL is slowly increased in proportional to the rate of charge.
 
• **Step input is not a constantly changing signal hence the output signal is constantly charging up and the signal is a ramp.**
